rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The essay at a glance "Humility" by Yuval Noah Harari is a historian's demolition of self-importance: most people, he argues, believe themselves the centre of the universe — their nation the most important, their religion the true one, their story the main plot of history — and the belief is not only false but catastrophic.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Most cultures claim centrality — Harari mocks this self-importance with examples.
Humility means accepting one's culture is not the centre of history.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: Apply to self: the same humility applies to individuals and nations — one personal application line lifts the answer.  ·  ## The themes worth an essay **The illusion of centrality** — the central theme: the universal human habit of placing one's own group at the axis of history, and the comparative proof that the habit, not the claim, is what is universal. **Humility as proportion** — the conceptual heart: humility defined as accurate self-measurement rather than self-abasement; the essay's constructive contribution.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## NEB short answers, solved **Q. What illusion does Harari say most people live under? (2 marks)** A. The illusion of centrality: the belief that one's own nation, religion, culture or self is the most important element of the human story. He shows by comparison that every group tells itself the same flattering story — which proves the story is a habit, not a truth. **Q.…  ·  ## NEB long answers, solved **Q. "Every culture thinks it is the centre of the universe — and that is why none is." Explain Harari's argument. rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. What is Harari's definition of humility? (2 marks) — recognising that your culture and self are not the centre of the universe.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Humility: cultural mirror (classified)** | Culture | Self-image | Harari’s point | |---|---|---| | Most nations | Centre of moral drama | Everyone claims the lead role | | Israelis | Chosen people narrative | Even small nations feel central | | Chinese | Middle Kingdom | Name itself claims centrality | | Europeans | Civilisers of the world | Mission as excuse |  ·  **Essay craft moves** | Move | Example | Effect | |---|---|---| | Provocation | Nobody is humble | Reader reacts | | Examples | Maps, myths, names | Pattern across cultures | | Irony | Pride in humility | Exposes contradiction | | Reflection | Moral progress question | Open ending |

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The argument, step by step The essay opens on the diagnosis: nearly everyone overestimates their own centrality. Harari frames it as a universal illusion — the belief that my group, my story, my suffering and my triumphs are the axis of history — and illustrates it with the mirror trick: every culture's history textbook places itself at the centre, which is statistically impossible and psychologically universal.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Satire** — the essay's master tone: the self-important patriot and the centre-of-history culture are held up until their symmetry makes the absurdity visible; the humour is analytic, not mocking for its own sake.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Harari's point: most cultures wrongly believe they are the centre of history — humility means accepting one's own partial view; state the thesis.  ·  Trick 2: He mocks the self-importance of every civilisation (Europe, China, India, Islam) — pick two of his examples of ethnocentrism.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. Give one example of cultural self-importance he criticises. (1 mark) — the European belief that history culminated in Western civilisation.
